Mr. Arthur was seventy-two years old and as set in his ways as a fence post in red clay. He lived out by the Scuppernong River in a house with a tin roof that sounded like a snare drum every time a summer shower rolled through. Now, Mr. Arthur had one great pride in this world, and that was his scuppernong vine. It grew over an arbor he had built himself with cedar posts, and every September that vine produced grapes so sweet and heavy they’d make your teeth ache just looking at 'em. Every year, Mr. Arthur made two dozen jars of scuppernong jelly, and every year, a raccoon he named Barnaby made it his personal mission to steal the best ones right off the vine before they were half ripe. Mr. Arthur tried everything. He hung shiny pie tins that spun in the breeze, he sprinkled red pepper flakes all around the roots, and one time he even stayed up half the night sitting on his porch in his rocking chair with a flashlight and a broom. But Barnaby was smarter than the average coon. That raccoon would just sit up in the forks of the pecan tree, wash his little hands, and watch Mr. Arthur like he was the entertainment. Well, one Tuesday morning in late August, Mr. Arthur walked out to check the grapes with his coffee cup in his hand, and he stopped dead in his tracks. Not a single grape was left on the north side of the arbor. But right there in the dirt under the vine wasn't raccoon tracks at all. It was size-eleven boot prints with a waffle tread. Mr. Arthur’s face turned the color of a ripe plum. He didn't have a thief in the woods; he had a thief in the neighborhood. So he decided to set a trap. He picked the three biggest, fattest, most purple scuppernongs left on the vine, gently hollowed them out with a paring knife, and filled every single one of 'em right to the brim with hot prepared horseradish. Then he hung them right out front where any passing bandit couldn't possibly miss 'em, and he went back inside to watch through the kitchen window. About noon, down the dirt road comes Mr. Cager Barnes, who lived a mile down the way and had a well-known sweet tooth and a lazy streak a mile wide. Cager walked right up to the arbor, looked both ways, and popped all three of those horseradish grapes straight into his mouth at the exact same time. Mr. Arthur watched from the window as Cager’s eyes went as big as Mason jar lids. Cager didn't yell, and he didn't run. He just stood there frozen for three solid seconds, turned completely red in the face, and then bolted sideways right through a patch of thick briars like a startled buck. The next morning, a brown paper bag was sitting on Mr. Arthur’s porch step. Inside was a fresh jar of blackberry jam and a note written in pencil on the back of a feed store receipt that said: Truce. The grapes belong to you, Arthur. And from that day to this, Mr. Arthur and Cager never spoke another word about the arbor, but Cager always tipped his hat real low whenever he walked past the river.
